news.title: Briefing · AI
news.intro1: From the collected posts the AI writes one briefing — not a summary per post, but the overall picture.
news.intro2: Two stages with two providers: Gemini watches the YouTube videos first (the only provider that opens a video URL itself, with its own key). What comes out of that goes, together with the text items, to
news.intro2b: which writes the briefing. If Gemini fails the briefing is still produced — just without video content.
news.intro3: The video is the expensive part, not the text: it is billed by video length. Subtitles would be cheaper, but YouTube no longer serves them to signed-out clients (checked 16 Aug 2026, yt-dlp included).
news.autoHint: Daily or weekly at the configured hour. Off: by button only. Posts are collected daily regardless.
news.topicsHint: One chapter per topic. The crypto part also gets the Marktradar readings (Fear & Greed, dominance, funding, long/short).
news.researchHint: With a Perplexity key the briefing additionally researches each topic on the web (sources included); with an xAI key, X sources are fetched via Grok — once a day. Both keys live under Access. Without a key the respective step is skipped silently.
news.grokModel: Grok model for the X search:
news.videosHint: Video is the most expensive input type — billed by length. 0 = watch no videos; the briefing then uses only titles and video descriptions.
news.reportModelHint: Empty = your globally configured provider. The briefing is pure text work — a cheaper model often does just as well.
news.resolutionHint: Low costs about 100 tokens per second of video, standard about 300 — three times as much. For spoken market commentary low is enough, because the audio carries the content.
news.costSplit: per run — of which {text} for the text, {n} × {proVideo} for the videos (at 20 minutes each)
news.layoutHint: Combined puts the most important items on top as cards (“top items”, at most three) and sets the rest as articles inside their chapter. Newspaper drops cards entirely, Tiles shows everything as equally sized cards, as before. Which items go on top is decided by the AI as it writes — if it marks none as important, the card row stays empty.
news.scopeHint: Items are the individual points of a chapter — in the newspaper layout, one article each with headline, paragraph and sources. The token cap bounds how long the AI answer may get; it caps the cost rather than setting it.
news.videoTokensHint: own output cap, empty = per level
news.topicChartanalyse: Technical chart analysis top 5 (from sources, with images)
news.customHint: Tone, focus and exclusions for the briefing — applies from the next run. Empty = unchanged.
news.customPlaceholder: e.g.: Write more tersely, no filler. Give the time of each item. Regulation only matters to me when it affects futures. More detail on Ether than on altcoins.
news.customLimits: {n} of {max} characters. The ground rules stay in force: no trade recommendations, no price targets, no forecasts, nothing invented. Every character costs tokens on every run.

benachrichtigungen.hinweis_kiBerichtFertig: A report or agent run has finished.

benachrichtigungen.hinweis_neueVersion: A newer release is published on GitHub.

hype.quadrantHinweis: Top right, trading is following along. Top left, there is talk the market does not follow — that is where bought noise sits. Labelled are the checked finds: green from a safety score of 70, amber from 40, red below; red with a name are the rejected ones. The grey ones stayed under the threshold and were never checked — hover to see their name.
hype.redditHinweis: needs an access token since OAuth became mandatory
hype.regelnBoerse: For Coin Radar favourites (Bitunix symbols): there is no liquidity pool and no contract check there — turnover, spread and funding are watched instead.
hype.rolleHinweis_editor: writes the report; this is where quality comes from
hype.rolleHinweis_research: searches the web per candidate — Perplexity brings its own search
hype.schluesselFehlt: Missing credentials: {anbieter}. Please add them in the AI settings.
hype.sicherheitHinweis: Anything breaching these never reaches the report — regardless of its hype score.
hype.trittbrettHilfe: Finds whose name contains an established coin or a foreign brand — they bring no idea of their own, only the hope of being mistaken for it. Their score is already reduced.
hype.wachhundHinweis: Watches the favourites on a schedule and fires when something material changes. Critical repeats after 1 hour at the earliest, the rest after 4.
hype.webhookPayload: The webhook posts JSON with regel, schwere, symbol, meldung and daten — a Home Assistant automation filters on trigger.json.schwere == 'kritisch' and starts the lights.

marktradar.title: Market radar — the lay of the land before you dig in
marktradar.intro: This page answers a single question: what shape is the market in right now? It is deliberately coarse. For the detailed view there are Bookmap, the liquidation map and open interest.

sections.p: Use "Cards" to decide what you see. Hidden cards are not loaded at all — they cost neither space nor requests to the data sources. The selection is per device: a lean view on the phone, the full set on the desktop.

The handle in the top left drags a card somewhere else. The bottom right corner makes it wider or taller, and a double click on that corner restores the default size. Order, size and visibility live in the browser of each device, not in the database. The page may therefore look different on the phone than on the desktop, and a fresh browser starts with the default arrangement.

Clicking the magnifier opens the same card in the full window — the same component with the same data, only with more room. It costs no extra request. Enlarged, many cards show more than they do small: longer history, tables instead of just the headline figure, extra switches. The source of the numbers is always stated at the bottom. Esc or a click beside the card closes it again.

The top right of every card says when the numbers are from. The dot next to it is green for fresh data and amber when the source could not be reached — you then keep seeing the last good state instead of an empty card. Red means nothing is available at all. The dot in the page header summarises all cards; if it is amber, some card below is showing a stale state.

Each card has its own cadence, matched to its source: funding, RSI and liquidations every minute, market overview and long/short every five, Fear & Greed every fifteen, rainbow and Pi Cycle only twice a day. Asking more often would change nothing there, because those sources themselves only produce daily or weekly values. "Refresh all" at the top right forces a pass; the arrow on a card reloads just that one.

sections.h: SETTING THE SYMBOL FROM THE RADAR
sections.p: In funding, the RSI heatmap, the market overview and altcoin season, clicking a row or a dot sets the symbol for the whole live analysis. Bookmap, liquidation map and open interest then show exactly that market. That is how the page is meant to be used: something stands out here, you examine it in detail there.

A sentiment index by alternative.me, built from volatility, volume, surveys and search trends. It measures mood, not price, and changes once a day. Next to the value you get yesterday's reading, the 30-day average and the low and high of the selected period. Extreme readings are more interesting than the middle — but "extreme fear" is not a buy signal, only the description of a state, and that state can stay extreme for weeks. Mostly useful as an input to position size and in comparison with the regime card further down.

What share of the entire crypto market belongs to Bitcoin. The curve comes from our own store — about six years of history, imported once from CoinMarketCap and updated daily; three series are shown: Bitcoin, Ethereum and all the rest. The spot value comes from the same series, with CoinGecko only as a fallback. Reading: rising dominance with falling prices means a flight out of altcoins into BTC; falling dominance with rising prices means fresh money is spreading out. In practice: an altcoin long against rising dominance is swimming upstream, however good the coin's chart looks.

The payment between longs and shorts on Binance perpetuals. The payment interval is not the same everywhere — eight hours is the norm, but many markets pay every four hours; "p.a." extrapolates using each market's actual interval so you can judge the magnitude. Positive means longs pay shorts — the long side is crowded. The card shows the extremes on both sides and, below, your own markets. Two things to take away: funding is a real cost — at +100 % p.a. holding eats into your margin — and an extreme reading tells you where the crowd sits, not when it will turn.

The Binance account ratio for the selected symbol, hourly over 48 hours, together with the 24-hour change in open interest and price. Important: it counts ACCOUNTS, not capital — a whale weighs the same as a tiny account, so the ratio mostly pictures retail. The combination is what matters: a lopsided ratio plus growing open interest means one side is loading up — then look at the liquidation map to see where the other side keeps its stops.

The only tile that looks outside the crypto market — and therefore the only one that can explain a move whose cause does not sit here at all. It shows the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures, the dollar index and the stablecoin flow. Three notes: first, these are deliberately FUTURES and not cash indices — the index stands still overnight and on weekends while the future trades nearly around the clock; a frozen value is tagged "closed". Second, the headline is the COUPLING (correlation of daily returns BTC↔Nasdaq over 30 days), not the price: "Nasdaq −1 %" only means something if your market is currently tied to it, and that coupling varies a lot. Third, colour shows tailwind or headwind FOR CRYPTO rather than the direction of the market itself — a rising dollar appears red because a strong dollar means tighter global liquidity. The stablecoin flow is deliberately the change in USDT and USDC supply, not "USDT dominance": the latter rises arithmetically whenever crypto falls and merely restates the price drop, while supply shows real money flowing in or being pulled out. The enlarged view does show dominance — but only DECOMPOSED. An example with round numbers: a total market of 2170bn including 245bn of stablecoins gives 11.3 % dominance. If the rest of the market falls 10 % without a single USDT being minted or redeemed, dominance reads 12.4 % — a jump of 1.1 points although not one dollar moved. That is why the tile splits the change into "from real flows" and "from price moves"; the two add up exactly to the total change. If the price part alone accounts for the swing, it was an optical illusion. Conversely a genuine inflow can coincide with FALLING dominance during a rally — the split makes that visible too.

Condenses four measurements of the selected symbol into one market state: price and OI change over a selectable window (15m/1h/4h), the current funding rate, and the liquidated long/short volume from the journal's own recording. The state is rule-based — the same numbers always yield the same verdict, no AI involved. "Long squeeze risk" for example means: longs pay high funding and keep loading up, but price does not follow — that side hangs lopsided. "Deleveraging" means: OI is collapsing and liquidations are spiking, the unwind is ALREADY running. In the enlarged view, chips show which factors carried the verdict, and on request the configured AI explains the situation in a few sentences — as context, explicitly without a trading recommendation; it never decides the state itself. For symbols outside the recorded top markets the liquidation factor is missing; the remaining rules still judge and the tile says honestly what was missing.

Wilder's RSI(14) from closed Binance candles, one dot per market, sorted left to right by turnover. The dashed line is the average of all shown markets — and that is the real value of this card: an oversold coin while the average is equally low is nothing of its own, just the market. What stands out is whatever deviates from the average. Switchable between the highest-turnover markets and the markets you traded yourself over the last 90 days.

The top 100 by market capitalisation without stablecoins, from CoinGecko. In bubble mode the area is the STRENGTH of the move — so a small coin doing 30 % stands out too. In tile mode the area is market capitalisation — so you can see whether the move carries any weight. The question answered here: is the whole market running, or just one corner of it? Not every coin has a Binance perpetual; where none exists, the symbol cannot be set.

Forced liquidations of the last 24 hours from the journal's own recording — there is no usable free third-party source, so the recording has to be switched on in the settings and only starts from then. Two exchanges are recorded: Binance sends at most one event per second per symbol (a sample — ratios are meaningful, absolute totals too low), while Bybit delivers its stream unthrottled and therefore usually contributes most of the total; the enlarged view shows the share per exchange. Red means a LONG was closed out, green a SHORT.

How many of the large altcoins with a perpetual market beat Bitcoin over the selected window, calculated from Binance daily candles. Above 75 is altcoin season, below 25 Bitcoin season — both thresholds come from the original index; they are set, not derived. The window changes the verdict considerably; when in doubt compare two windows before drawing a conclusion.

A logarithmic curve fitted to Bitcoin's entire price history, with bands from "fire sale" to "bubble". The thing to understand: the bands shift with every new price because the fit is recalculated — what counts as "cheap" today can be the middle band a year from now. A usable mood gauge across years, far too coarse for a trading decision.

When the 111-day moving average crosses the doubled 350-day average from below, that historically landed close to a cycle top. The card shows the distance between the two lines and whether a crossing has triggered. Three hits in three opportunities is an observation, not a rule — treat it as an early warning to be careful with leverage, not as an exit signal.

The only card that is about you rather than the market: your own trades are grouped by the Fear & Greed value of their entry day, calculated on net results after fees, bot trades excluded. Per phase you get count, hit rate, total, average, profit factor and long share. Faded phases have too few trades to mean anything. If, across many trades, you consistently lose in a particular market state, that is the most concrete rule this whole page can give you.

The card that reads all the others. Pressing "Summarise the situation" sends the numbers CURRENTLY on screen — sentiment, dominance, funding, long/short, liquidations, RSI, breadth, cycle models, macro and your own record per market phase — to the configured AI and returns a read in five lines: an overall state, three to five points, the contradictions between the cards and at most three things to watch. Enlarged, "Basis" lists every line the AI was given, so the summary can be checked rather than believed. Important: it looks nothing up and must not give a trading recommendation; it only orders what is on the screen anyway. It is only ever generated by pressing the button — neither the page timer nor "Refresh all" triggers an AI request, and a read younger than twenty minutes is reused instead of paid for again. A second run is the small arrow inside the card. Which provider answers is set under Settings → AI.

News first — what is scheduled today. Then the radar — what shape is the market in, and does that fit what I intend to do. Then set a symbol and go into detail in bookmap, liquidation map or open interest. The reverse order — chart first, justification afterwards — reliably ends with you hunting for the card that agrees with the opinion you already had.

None of these cards is a signal. They answer what tailwind you are travelling with, not when to click. Used sensibly they change position size, holding time and the question of whether to trade against the market at all today — the trigger still comes from your strategy.

marktradar.caveat: Every number here comes from third parties who promise nothing. If a source fails you see the last known state with its timestamp — check that date before you act on it. And remember: extreme readings can stay extreme. Sentiment, funding and dominance tell you where the market stands, not where it goes next.

bookmap.title: Bookmap — order book and trading in real time
bookmap.intro: This view shows only MEASURED data: the actual Binance order book and actually executed trades. Nothing here is calculated or estimated.

sections.p: Each horizontal cell is resting liquidity — limit orders waiting at that price. Bright means a lot. A continuous bright band is a large order sitting there over time, and such bands often act as resistance because price has to work through them.

One column is exactly one pixel wide and covers the configured interval. At one second per column, a 1200-pixel window shows twenty minutes. A grey vertical stripe marks a gap — the tab was in the background and the connection was closed.

The mid price between best bid and best ask. It comes from the order book, not from completed trades, so it usually sits slightly beside the trade dots. At very tight zoom you can see its steps — those are individual ticks.

Executed trades. Area is the traded quantity, colour is the aggressive side: green means buyers lifted the offer, red means sellers hit the bid. The "group trade dots" slider bundles them in time — without it they merge into a band.

When bubbles pile up at a bright band but the mid price does not get through, absorption is happening: someone is taking the pressure without price giving way. If the line then does break through, a fast move often follows because the resistance is gone.
Real forced liquidations from the Binance stream. Unlike the liquidation map, these are not estimates but events that actually happened.
The volume profile of the visible period: how much was traded at which prices, split by buy and sell. Hovering shows quantity and value. The width is adjustable; at zero it disappears.
Traded volume per time slice, green when buyers were more aggressive. The switch from green to red shows a change of initiative — hard to see in the bubbles alone.
The dashed "snapshot reach" line marks how deep the fetched order book goes. Above and below it the picture is incomplete, not empty — orders do exist there, we just cannot see them.

Both live in the side menu on the left. At the top you choose futures (perpetual) or spot, below that you search for the symbol. The choice applies to the whole live analysis: the liquidation map and open interest follow the same symbol, and a click in the market radar sets it too. Perp and spot have separate order books — for the same coin they look different, and that is not a bug.

"Price band" sets how far the map reaches above and below the mid price: tight shows the inner workings of the book, wide shows the big blocks. "ms per column" sets how much time goes into one pixel, and therefore the length of the visible window — 1000 ms is twenty minutes across 1200 pixels, 250 ms is five. Small values for execution, large ones for the overview.

Top right switches the palette (Viridis, Classic, Journal) — pure taste. More important is the scale in the side menu: "Automatic" adjusts brightness continuously so there is always something to see; "Fixed value" makes pictures comparable over time, because the same quantity always gets the same colour. The small button beside it adopts the current automatic value as a starting point. The "liquidity threshold" hides everything below a given share — turn it up until only the clumps remain.

"Group trade dots" bundles trades into bubbles and controls spacing and size at once: small means many fine dots, precise in time; large means few fat bubbles and a coarser picture. Separately switchable are the volume profile on the right including its lane width, the liquidation diamonds (futures only) and the volume bars below. If you want recording to continue while the tab is in the background, switch off "pause in background" — that keeps the connection open permanently and costs CPU time.

"Pause" freezes the display only; recording continues — useful to study something without it scrolling away to the left. "Auto axis" makes the price axis follow the mid price; a double click in the chart resets it if you got lost while dragging.

In the journal, a trade in the daily view can open the order book at its entry time, provided a recording exists for that window. The view then switches to replay mode: the slider at the bottom moves through the recorded window, the header shows the period, and "leave replay" takes you back to the live picture. That is how you find out after the fact what was actually resting in the book when you entered.

Not for finding ideas, but for executing them. The idea comes from the chart or the strategy: "I want to go long at this level". Bookmap then tells you whether anything is actually resting there, whether it holds while being traded against, and whether it gets swept or pulled. The same for exits: a thick band in front of your target is a reason to leave early rather than hope it breaks.

Three that everyone makes once. First: treating a large band as a promise — it can vanish the moment price arrives. Second: reading colour as an absolute while the scale is on "Automatic" and keeps rescaling; comparing pictures requires a fixed value. Third: mistaking the gap after a background pause for a quiet market — the grey stripe means "not measured", not "nothing happened".

bookmap.caveat: What you see can change in seconds: limit orders can be pulled at any time. A large band is a statement of intent, not a promise — it may vanish as soon as price approaches.

levmap.title: Liquidation map — where positions would be force-closed
levmap.intro: This view is a MODEL, not a measurement. Binance does not publish position data. All that is known is how many contracts are open in total — from that, likely liquidation prices are estimated.

sections.p: For each candle the change in open interest is examined. If it rises, positions were opened — somewhere within that candle's price range, so the increase is spread evenly across it rather than placed at a point. If it falls, positions were closed and the existing stock is thinned proportionally.

Whether an increase was long or short is decided by the candle's aggressive buy volume. If buyers dominate, the increase counts mostly as long. This is an approximation — nobody but the exchange knows the actual split.
The snapshot: long zones to the left, short zones to the right, centre line at the current price. Bar length is the value in dollars, linearly normalised — twice as long means twice as much.

Time to the right, price upward, colour shows zone mass. Candles are drawn on top, and their wicks show exactly the touches that sweep a zone. On the right is the distribution profile of the current state.

Once price has run through a zone it turns grey — retroactively across its whole history. Only what still stands today, and could still trigger, stays coloured. Without this recolouring every zone ever created would glow forever and the map would become unreadable over time.

The controls sit in the side menu on the left. At the top you switch between "distribution" and "history": distribution answers "where does it sit now", history answers "how did it build up and what has already been swept". For a decision in the moment the distribution is enough; to understand a move you need the history.

"All" mixes them weighted. A single tier is a what-if: if everyone used this leverage, the zones would sit here. 100x hugs the price, 10x sits about ten percent away. Useful when you want to know which part of a clump comes from short-term leverage and which from patient positions further out.

The time window decides how far back positions are attributed — it is the control with the greatest effect on the map. Short windows are current but cover little; long windows cover more but drag along zones whose holders left long ago. The span below sets the price range shown around the current price; in the chart the mouse wheel zooms continuously.

In the history view the zone threshold hides weak zones — turn it up until only the clumps remain, because those are the point of the map. The profile width controls the distribution lane on the right edge; at 0 it disappears and the history gets the full area.

The share of the position the exchange requires to remain as collateral. At 100x leverage and a 0.4 percent rate you may only lose 0.6 percent, not one percent — which is why 100x liquidates at minus 0.6 percent. The rate depends on the coin: 0.004 is BTCUSDT tier 1, small coins sit closer to one to five percent. That is why it is fetched per symbol — from Binance or Bybit, whose values differ by up to half. "Manual" puts one fixed value back in place for every coin; every zone then sits too close to the price for anything but BTC and ETH. Tier 1 is always used: the map does not know position sizes, and above the cap shown in the sidebar the real rate rises.

The most important number in the legend: what share of the actual open interest is represented in the map at all. Positions opened before the time window are unknown to the model. Below twenty percent a warning appears — the map then shows only a fraction. The first response to low coverage is always: enlarge the time window.

Measured against 9,734 recorded real liquidations: the map marks about thirteen percent of the visited price range and catches roughly twenty percent of actual events within it. That is a factor of 1.54 over chance — measurably better than guessing, but four out of five liquidations happen elsewhere.

Two questions. First: where is the fuel? A thick clump above the price is a reason not to sell an advance too early — once touched, forced buying accelerates the move. Second: where do I NOT put my own stop? Sitting right behind a thick clump means being stopped out together with the crowd. A little further back costs slightly more risk and avoids the standard trap.

Neither a price target nor a schedule. Many zones are never touched; others are cleared in seconds without the expected move following. After a sweep the zone turns grey — anyone still waiting for "the liquidations above" is waiting for something that already happened. And because the model only estimates the side, the left-right split is the least certain thing on the whole map.

levmap.caveat: The biggest fiction: every contract has two sides, and the model assumes only one of each pair is leveraged. It also cannot see cross margin or added collateral. Read the map as "where is a lot compared to the surroundings", not as a price target.

oi.title: Open interest — how much capital is committed
oi.intro: Open interest is the total of all open contracts. It does not say whether the market is bullish or bearish — it says how much is on the table at all. Only together with price does it become meaningful.

sections.p: The blue area is open interest, the white line is price. They share the time axis but have separate scales — what matters is direction, not absolute levels.
The bars show how much was added or removed per time slice. Green means build-up, red means unwinding. The stock itself drifts slowly; the change shows when something actually happened.

Above the chart you get the change in open interest, the change in price and, derived from both, the reading in plain words. That is the short form of the four cases below — if you are in a hurry, that line is enough.
New long positions are carrying the move. This counts as a solid advance — fresh money is flowing in rather than old positions merely unwinding.
Shorts covering: sellers close their positions and must buy to do so. The rise is driven by compulsion, not conviction — such moves often stall once the covering is done.
New short positions. The decline is being actively traded, not just passively passed through.
Longs unwinding. Often seen at the end of a decline, when the last holders give up.

The symbol comes from the side menu and applies to the whole live analysis — change it here and bookmap and the liquidation map change too. Below it sits the only other control on this page: the time window. Short windows use five-minute resolution and reach back about 41 hours; longer ones step up to coarser periods automatically. The span actually achieved is shown in the header — it can be shorter than selected if the exchange does not serve data that far back.

Both pages use the same data. What appears here as an increase is distributed across prices there and converted into liquidation zones. A strong build-up without price movement means, for the map, that closely spaced zones are forming — and those later get cleared together.

As a cross-check, not as a trigger. You have a move on the chart and want to know whether it is carried: if open interest rises with it, new money is involved; if it falls, positions are merely unwinding and the move often ends where the unwinding ends. The second occasion is a quiet market with strongly growing interest — that is the setup where a jump comes later, because both sides have loaded up.

oi.caveat: Open interest is a net figure. If a thousand positions open and nine hundred close, it shows only a hundred — actual turnover is always larger than the curve suggests.

nachrichten.title: News — what is coming up and what was said
nachrichten.intro: Three parts, in the order you need them in the morning: the digest summarises, the calendar tells you when it gets rough, and the posts are the raw sources to read up on. This page does not replace a news service — it makes sure you do not trade into a release unaware.

sections.p: At the top is what the AI distilled from the posts of the last 36 hours: an assessment of the situation and below it the individual points with their source, important ones highlighted. It is generated automatically once at midday, or on demand by button (at most every five minutes). The footer states how many posts were read, which model was used and what it consumed. The "AI, unverified" mark is meant literally: this is a summary, not an established fact — for anything you put money on, click through to the original source beside it.

Economic events grouped by day. Each entry shows the time in your time zone, the currency area, the impact level plus forecast, actual and previous values. Yesterday deliberately stays visible so you can read the actual value of releases that already happened — how the market reacted to the last number is often more informative than the next forecast.

The raw sources, newest first, each linking to the original. The source row lets you hide individual providers — that affects the display only, they are still fetched; switching them off for good happens in the settings. How many items are loaded is set beside it; the digest always reads the last 36 hours regardless.

"Fetch posts" queries the sources immediately instead of waiting for the next scheduled pass (pressing it repeatedly hits a throttle — that is intentional, not a fault). "Generate digest" writes a new report using the AI model chosen in the settings; depending on the provider that costs quota or compute time.

Three filters, all remembered per device. The period sets how far ahead you look. Impact is a LOWER BOUND: "medium and up" includes the high ones, "high only" leaves a handful of events in a typical week, "all" around a hundred. For currency areas, "none selected" means all — anyone trading mainly crypto gets a long way with USD and JPY.

The vertical divider between calendar and posts can be dragged, as can the bottom edge of both lists; a double click on the handle resets the height. This too lives in the device's browser — on a phone the columns stack anyway.

sections.h: WHY THE CALENDAR GROWS OVER TIME
sections.p: The feed only ever carries the current week. The journal therefore collects every event it sees permanently instead of passing it through. Consequence: your own stock only reaches as far into the future as the source has switched over so far — the line below the list says until when. An empty second week means "not collected yet", not "nothing scheduled".

Around a high-impact event the problem is not direction but execution: the spread widens and single candles take out stops that would otherwise never be reached. Two sane stances: be flat beforehand, or keep the position small enough and the stop wide enough that the spike cannot catch you. You can always join later — what remains fifteen to thirty minutes after the number is usually the real move.

sections.h: WHERE IT SITS IN THE ROUTINE
sections.p: This page comes before the market radar. First: is there any reason to be careful today? Then: what shape is the market in, and finally the detail on one symbol. Done the other way round, you read the calendar after the stop has already been hit.

nachrichten.caveat: Summaries are produced by a language model and can be wrong or leave out something important — always check the original source before deciding. Event times and impact levels come from a third-party feed, get rescheduled at short notice and are equally unverified. None of this is investment advice.

agent.title: Strategies — how the workflow fits together
agent.intro: This area runs trading strategies automatically: on paper first, and only later — after several approvals — for real. The safe path is always the same: build → measure → observe → only then money.

sections.p: Under "New strategy" you will find ready-made templates (LSOB, MACD cloud, Bollinger+RSI and more) — adopting a template is the fastest start. Your own ideas are assembled from building blocks in the strategy editor, or described in plain words to the chat builder; both produce the same kind of rule set, not program code.

sections.h: 2 · Create an instance — always paper first
sections.p: An instance is a strategy with concrete settings: symbols, timeframe, parameters and risk (risk per trade, daily loss limit, minimum reward/risk). Always start in "paper" mode — the engine then trades simulated money, every 15 seconds, on closed candles.

sections.h: 3 · Measure in the lab before you start
sections.p: The backtest checks your settings against the past — with the same engine as paper trading, including fees and slippage. The most important number is the expectancy per trade in R; below roughly 30 trades a result is not reliable.

A setting that only looks good in the period you picked it in is worthless. The multi test therefore splits the period into two halves — optimisation and verification — and runs several symbols. Adopt a change only if it is better in EVERY cell.

After starting, "Setups" shows what the strategy detects and why setups get discarded (zone broken, reward/risk too low …). "Performance" shows the key figures, the setup funnel, and the timeline chart draws what the agent saw and traded on the price chart.

sections.h: 6 · Put the AI agent to work
sections.p: The "Optimise with AI agent" button (on the instances page and in the lab) hands an instance to the AI coach. It reads the performance data, tests counter-hypotheses in backtests and files an improvement suggestion. Suggestions NEVER change anything on their own — you accept or discard them in the lab.

Before live comes shadow mode: the full live path runs, but the order is only logged. Real trading requires three separate approvals — the global switch in settings, the per-instance approval and enough paper trades. Any trading-relevant change revokes the approval again.

The red emergency stop on the instances page halts all instances immediately and can close open positions. While it is active no instance can be started — it is deliberately lifted only in settings, never by a start click.

agent.caveat: Beta: this area is under development and not investment advice. Backtest numbers are not a promise — a result only counts once it holds outside the period it was chosen on. Let a strategy run on paper long enough before even thinking about live.

livetrading.title: Live trading — the workspace during a session
livetrading.intro: The tile grid for the hours you actually trade. Its own layout, independent of the market radar, and a check interval of three seconds instead of thirty so fast tiles refresh on time. Desktop only — an order book and a candle chart cannot be operated on 375 pixels. Can be switched off under Settings → Live.

sections.p: Above the tile area sits the session bar: maximum loss, maximum number of trades and your intent are entered BEFORE starting and cannot be changed afterwards — deliberately, because a plan you can revise mid-trade is no plan at all.

Starting opens the page in its own window in cockpit state (no side menu, no navigation, full width) so nothing else is within reach during a session. True fullscreen is a button, not an automatism — the browser only allows it after a click inside the new window. If a popup blocker intervenes, it continues in the current tab.

Same mechanics as the market radar: drag by the handle top-left, resize at the bottom-right corner, double-click to reset. Visibility, order and size live in the device's browser. Each tile has its own interval (the liquidation ticker five seconds, positions ten, indices and calendar one minute); every three seconds it checks whether one is due.

Computed in the browser from the stored time zones, with no fetch: which session (Asia, Europe, US) is currently running, the countdown to the next market mark, and the volatility windows. Each session carries its own zone as wall-clock time, because the US and Europe switch to summer time weeks apart.

Market mechanics is the same rule-based tile as in the market radar, here on a 15-minute window. The liquidation ticker shows the latest forced liquidations from our own recording, out of an in-memory ring buffer — that shows "what just happened", while the database is only written every 30 seconds.

The positions tile reads the open and closed positions of the running session from Bitunix and computes the session state against the plan limits — realised and unrealised stay separate, and the limits count only against the realised part. The calendar countdown shows the next economic events of the coming hours from our own calendar store.

Indices shows ES=F, NQ=F and the dollar index as intraday candles from Yahoo. Funding, long/short + open interest and the macro environment are the same tiles as in the market radar — funding and long/short follow the symbol choice.

The two large work surfaces: the bookmap on Binance's live order-book stream, the leverage map as a model based on our own recording. Neither has an enlarged view — that would be a second connection — and both need at least two columns of width. Full explanations live in the dedicated "Order book" and "Liquidation map" views.

The same AI tile as in the market radar: it reads the current state of the other tiles and interprets it. It is generated by button only — the three-second interval never triggers an AI request, otherwise every session would cost a fortune.

livetrading.caveat: The third-party figures (indices, funding, calendar) promise nothing and can go stale — the dot on the tile tells you how fresh they are. The leverage map is a model, not a measurement. This page is a tool, not a signal generator: your strategy still supplies the trigger.

liveSessions.title: Session archive — what became of your intentions
liveSessions.intro: Every finished trading session as its own entry. The key figure is not P&L but whether the plan held: a winning session that broke its loss limit is luck, a losing one within limits was good work.

sections.p: The headline number is the share of sessions in which the plan held — not the sum of profits. Judging by P&L alone rewards luck and punishes good execution that met bad luck.
Sessions can be archived instead of deleted. The discipline rate deliberately keeps counting archived ones — a number you could improve by tidying up would be worthless.
Not a market but a span of time: the symbol may change during the session, every switch lands in the log, and the session follows the last symbol picked — that is what the replay needs.
The replay button only becomes active once an order-book recording actually exists for that symbol and period. Then the book from the session can be stepped through again frame by frame.

liveSessions.caveat: The archive shows how you traded, not whether a strategy is any good — that is what the evaluation is for. Without recording switched on there is no replay.

liveAuswertung.title: Session evaluation — four questions that build on each other
liveAuswertung.intro: Four questions about your trading sessions that build on each other: do I keep my plan and am I improving, does the plan help at all, at which times do I trade well, and does it turn with duration or trade count.

sections.p: Do I keep my plan, and does the rate improve over time? The first and most important question — everything else builds on it.
Do sessions with a held plan actually do better than those that broke it? Only if yes is the plan more than a ritual.
At which times of day do I trade well? Grouped by session start, so systematically bad windows show up.
Does the result turn the longer a session lasts or the more trades it contains? The classic over-trading question.
Groups with fewer than four sessions are greyed out: three sessions on a Tuesday are noise, not a finding. The computation lives in its own network-free module and is covered by a self-test.

liveAuswertung.caveat: An evaluation is only as good as the number of sessions behind it — greyed-out groups are not yet a statement. It describes your behaviour; it is not investment advice.

hypeRadar.title: Hype radar — what is being hyped right now, and what of it has substance
hypeRadar.intro: The radar searches several sources for young coin projects, scores them by fixed rules and checks them hard for fraud patterns — only then does a language model write a report about the few that survive. Everything here is research, not investment advice.

sections.p: Stage 1 collects finds from CoinGecko, DexScreener and GeckoTerminal. Stage 2 computes a hype score. Stage 3 checks every candidate for fraud patterns. Only stage 4 calls a language model — and only for the best few. Having an AI judge five hundred raw finds would be slow, expensive and slightly different every run; a computed ranking can be checked.

sections.h: SCANNING IS FREE, THE REPORT IS NOT
sections.p: "Scan only" runs stages 1 to 3 and costs nothing. "Scan & report" adds the AI — a few cents to about a franc per run, depending on the chosen tier. If the safety check leaves no usable candidate, no model is called at all.

sections.h: WHAT MAKES UP THE HYPE SCORE
sections.p: Five sub-scores: how much is being said, whether trading follows, how many independent sources the find came from, whether it fits a current theme, and how young the trading pair is. Weighting is configurable; the sub-scores are shown per find so the number stays traceable.

sections.h: THE NUMBER OF SOURCES MATTERS MOST
sections.p: A paid campaign fills one source, rarely three independent ones. So multi-source confirmation weighs heavily — and bought visibility (such as a paid slot on DexScreener) counts explicitly less than genuine engagement. Otherwise you could buy your way into the report.

Horizontally: is trading picking up. Vertically: how much is being said. Top right both move together — real momentum. Top left people talk but the market does not follow: that is where bought noise sits, and it is the field a sorted list cannot show. Colour and shape show the check result, so the distinction never rests on colour alone.

The small pale dots are finds below the minimum score — never checked. They are shown on purpose: only against that field can you see whether a candidate really stands out. On many days only a handful clear the threshold.

sections.h: THE STAGE THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS IS USEFUL
sections.p: Thousands of tokens launch daily, and a sizeable share is built so buyers cannot get out again. Checked are sell locks, mintability, sell taxes, whether liquidity is locked, and the distribution of the largest holders — via GoPlus, and via RugCheck as a fallback on Solana.

Hard criteria reject immediately, regardless of hype: a token you cannot exit does not get better because everyone talks about it. Soft findings only lower the safety score. Important: if no data can be fetched, the find counts as unverified and therefore rejected — unverified is not a free pass.

sections.h: EVEN MANY BUYS CAN BE A WARNING
sections.p: Twenty buys per sell looks like buying pressure — but it is also the signature of a trap nobody exits. So a very one-sided trading pattern gives a deduction, not a bonus.
Every rejected find keeps its reason, shown in the report. Without it you could not answer why a much-discussed coin is missing — and that question decides whether you trust the radar.

sections.h: PIN WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP AN EYE ON
sections.p: A find disappears with the next run. The star pins it; the chip above opens live tiles with price, liquidity, volume and buy/sell ratio, fetched fresh and reloaded periodically. The scores next to them come from the last run and are labelled as such — they are not live data.

sections.h: THE WATCHDOG LOOKS WHILE YOU DO NOT
sections.p: On a schedule it compares every favourite against its last state: price move, daily move, liquidity outflow and the safety check. The trigger was a real case — a find looked passable at 44,000 USD liquidity during the scan and had 2,400 left at the next look. Between two glances at the page, a find can die.

Incoming liquidity is pleasant but not a call to act. And the safety rule only reports the transition from "passed" to "rejected" — pinning an already rejected find is a known state, and repeating it would be noise without news.
The same rule fires again after an hour at the earliest (critical) or four hours otherwise, else a volatile meme coin becomes a siren. Individual favourites can be muted: still watched, but silent.

Alerts always appear in the app. In addition ntfy, Telegram and a webhook can be enabled — each with its own minimum severity, so not every price hop wakes the phone at night. The test button sends a harmless message through every enabled channel.

The webhook posts JSON with rule, severity, symbol and message — meant for a webhook trigger in Home Assistant. An automation there filters on severity "critical" and does whatever it likes: a push, an announcement, or a red light.

sections.h: WHERE DOES IT RUN, AND CAN I TRADE IT AT ALL
sections.p: Every find shows its decentralised venue (such as Raydium or Uniswap) and whether Bitunix, Bitget or Pionex list it — including the market type: F for futures, S for spot. A coin that only exists on spot can neither be leveraged nor shorted. A switch can filter the whole run to what is tradeable.
Futures exchanges bundle micro-priced coins into thousand-packs (1000PEPE, 1000SHIB). The check accounts for that — otherwise exactly the meme coins this is mostly about would count as unlisted.

The tiers assign three roles at once: a cheap model for helper tasks, one for per-candidate web research, and one for the report — that is where quality comes from. Note: "Thorough" usually beats "Simple" at the same profile in both depth AND price, because each research prompt is short instead of one long combined context. Under "Manual" the three roles can be set individually, including a local Ollama model.

sections.h: A MISSING KEY BLOCKS THE START
sections.p: If a chosen role has no credentials, the report button stays disabled and the page says why. Silently falling back to another provider would be worse: you would wonder about quality or the bill later and never find the reason. What each run actually cost is under Settings → AI → Overview.

On narrow devices the quadrant and the wide table are dropped — a scatter plot at 375 pixels is unreadable. Instead each find appears as a card with scores, theme, liquidity, age, exchanges and outcome. Favourites, live tiles, alerts and reports work unchanged.

coinRadar.title: Coin Radar — which of the tradable coins can be traded right now
coinRadar.intro: The Coin Radar walks the coins that are tradable on Bitunix and measurable on Binance and answers TWO separate questions: how much is going on right now (opportunity — ATR, RVOL, ADX, funding), and what an order actually costs (execution — slippage, depth, spread, measured against the real order books of Bitunix and Bitget). It is a description of state, not a forecast.

sections.p: That this page makes sense at all rests on a single observation: volatility in crypto is persistent. It comes in phases lasting weeks to months — what moved yesterday will very likely move again tomorrow. DIRECTION is not persistent. A ranking by movement therefore carries into the present; a ranking by who will rise would be tea leaves. That is exactly why there is not a single up-arrow on this page.

Among the headline figures is how well the previous run predicted this one (Spearman rank correlation, computed only over coins scored in both runs). Near 1 means the list holds and can be relied on. Near 0 means it is noise, and then it says nothing about the coming hours. The number sits deliberately beside the others rather than in the fine print — a ranking that hides its own predictive power is more dangerous than none.

sections.h: ATR % — IS AN ENTRY WORTH IT AT ALL
sections.p: The average range of the last 14 candles, divided by price. Relative to price, because absolute values say nothing: two dollars of swing is nothing for Bitcoin and everything for a cent coin. A coin with 0.2 % hourly ATR simply does not move enough for an entry with a stop — costs eat the range.

The last candle's volume relative to the average of the twenty before it. The coin is compared with ITSELF, not with others: a micro-cap at ten times its usual volume is an observation; the same absolute number for Bitcoin is a quiet afternoon. Above 2.0 counts as "in play" across the industry. It is computed against the PRECEDING candles — were the current one included in the baseline, a breakout would damp its own yardstick.

Trend strength without a direction claim: above 25 a move runs through, below 20 the price saws sideways. That decides which kind of trade fits at all — the same move is a trend ride in one regime and a losing game in a range. Coins below 20 get the hint "sawing sideways".

The funding rate, annualised. 0.01 % per eight hours sounds like nothing and is nearly 11 % a year. It enters INVERTED: expensive means few points. A coin whose holding cost eats the edge is not a good candidate, however handsomely it moves. If the rate is missing, it gets the middle and a hint — unknown is not the same as free.

sections.g: WHY SO MANY COINS DROP OUT
sections.h: LIQUIDITY IS A GATE, NOT A SCORE
sections.p: Of roughly 500 pairs, forty to fifty typically remain. That is intended: turnover and spread are knock-out criteria, not sub-scores. As a sub-score, illiquidity could be outvoted by the others — and then a coin would rank top where high movement only means every order moves the price itself. The size at the top of the book is collected and displayed but gates nobody by default: it depends on tick size and, when measured, rejected pairs with over 500M daily turnover. To see who failed on what, open "Failed the gates".

sections.h: UNKNOWN IS NEVER SCORED AS GOOD
sections.p: If a coin's spread is missing it drops out — not because it is bad, but because it is unchecked, and unchecked does not belong in a list claiming "you can get in and out here". Same for funding: no data means a middling score plus a hint, not full marks for "cheap".

The total score from 0 to 100 is the weighted average of the four sub-scores; the weights are free in the settings. Each sub-score appears in the expanded row as its own bar, along with the raw values per timeframe. A metric without a derivation is exactly the one people end up following blindly — which is why every score here can be opened and recomputed.

The coarser timeframe (1h by default) carries the score, the finer one (15m) confirms it. If both are "in play", there is a bonus and a check mark on the row. If they contradict each other, that is shown as a hint rather than averaged away: "only in play on 15m" means a short-lived spike, "already fading on 15m" means the move is over. Both are information an average would have destroyed.

Movement alone does not say whether a coin can be traded. So for every survivor the real order book is fetched and the cost of a 5,000 USD order computed — separately for buy and sell, because a book that makes entry cheap and exit expensive is a trap no average reveals. The "round trip" is the sum of both. For scale: BTC costs about 0.01 basis points, a thin coin over 45 — nearly half a percent just to get in and out again.

Opportunity and execution are not merged. Pressed into one score, a wild coin with an expensive book looks like a calm one with a cheap book — and that confusion costs money. If the amount does not fit the book at all, the execution score is ZERO rather than a deduction: someone who cannot get out has no execution problem, they have no execution.

Measured on Bitunix and Bitget; the cheaper one is shown. The differences are large — in the test run TREE cost 5 basis points on Bitunix and 54 on Bitget, ten times as much. Pionex is deliberately absent: it lists 405 spot markets and NO perpetuals, and the Coin Radar ranks perpetuals. There is nothing to measure there.

For each of the top twenty, what actually happened afterwards is recorded — after 15 minutes, one hour and four hours. What is measured is the SPAN between best and worst point, not the return: the page promises movement, not direction. What matters is the comparison with the bottom half — on a busy day everything moves, and without a control group even a random ranking would look brilliant. The weights are NOT auto-optimised against this; that would be the most comfortable way to fool yourself.

sections.h: A RUN IS FREE, THE SUMMARY COSTS A CENT
sections.p: "Measure now" takes about fifteen seconds and a small slice of the Binance budget — no money. Only the short AI summary above the table costs about a cent per run and can be switched off in the settings. The automation switch is off out of the box.

sections.h: STARS ARE SHARED WITH THE HYPE RADAR
sections.p: A pinned coin lands in the same favourites list as a Hype Radar find and is watched by the same watchdog. That is the point of two pages under one roof: one watchlist, whether a coin arrived via novelty or via tradability.

sections.h: AND WHAT THIS PAGE IS NOT
sections.p: Not a buy recommendation and not a claim about direction. A high score means: this coin can currently be traded — it moves, something is going on, you can get in and out. Whether up or down appears nowhere here, and cannot be derived from these numbers either.

pendente.title: Pending trades — what is open right now
pendente.intro: All open positions from the connected exchanges, polled on a schedule. This page is the bridge between exchange and journal: notes, ratings and attributes you record here move into the finished journal entry automatically when the position closes.

sections.p: Position, entry, leverage, margin and liquidation price come from the exchange unchanged — they are not recomputed. If something differs from the exchange's own screen, it is the polling moment, not a formula of ours.
The view polls regularly while open. It is a watch window, not a trading desk: entries and exits happen at the exchange or in the live-trading window.

Individual fills can be expanded per position. Needed because a scaled-in position shows at the exchange as one line with an average price — but the journal wants to know at which prices you actually bought.

sections.h: WRITE BEFORE, DO NOT INVENT AFTER
sections.p: Notes, attributes and the setup rating belong before the outcome. Afterwards you remember a loss differently than before — which is exactly why the place for them is here and not in the journal.
Once the position is closed and the trade is imported, the journal picks up what you recorded automatically — opening and closing note, attributes, satisfaction, stress and whether the plan held.

Grid and strategy bots appear as their own group, not among manual positions. They follow different rules: for them the reported quantity is already the total turnover, so they must be computed differently from an ordinary position.

coinradar.bestaetigtHilfe: In play on both timeframes — not just a short-lived spike.
coinradar.dauerhaftHinweis: How often a coin was in the top ten across recent runs. What survives several runs is more than a spike.
coinradar.eAktivHinweis: Off by default. A run costs nothing but a small slice of the Binance budget — still, it should not run unasked.
coinradar.eEinordnungHinweis: One paragraph on the overall picture, about a cent per run. The numbers are there anyway; the sentence says what they mean together.
coinradar.eGewichteHinweis: How strongly each sub-score enters the total. The sum need not be 100 — it is normalised anyway — but 100 reads as percent.
coinradar.eHuerdenHinweis: Fail one and the coin never enters the ranking. Liquidity is a gate, not a sub-score — otherwise an illiquid jitterbug could outvote the other scores.
coinradar.eMinTiefe: Minimum at top of book (0 = off)
coinradar.eTiefeHinweis: Off by default, deliberately: top of book is only the best bid and ask size, not market depth — how large it is depends on tick size. Against real data this gate rejected pairs with over 500M daily turnover and 0.5 bp spread because 5 dollars sat at the front. Turnover and spread do the work; the value is still collected and displayed.
coinradar.eZeiteinheitenHinweis: Two levels: the coarser one carries the score, the finer one confirms or contradicts it. A contradiction is shown, not averaged away.
coinradar.einordnungQuelle: Written by a language model from the numbers above — not a forecast, not trading advice.
coinradar.laufFertig: Done: {n} coins scored, {v} failed the gates.
coinradar.nochNichtsHinweis: "Measure now" walks the tradable universe once — about fifteen seconds, at no cost.
coinradar.passtNicht: On {b} the amount does not fit the book.
coinradar.spalteAusfuehrungHilfe: Execution quality: what a 5,000 USD order costs, measured against the real order book. NOT merged with opportunity.
coinradar.spalteNoteHilfe: Opportunity: how much is going on (ATR, RVOL, ADX, funding).
coinradar.spalteRundlaufHilfe: Entry and exit combined, in basis points. For scale: BTC sits at about 0.01.
coinradar.verlaufHinweis: Every run compares its ranking with the previous one. Near 1 means the list holds; near 0 means it is noise — and then it says nothing about tomorrow.
